Sight
SīT
n. (rendering Hebrew 'ayin and mar'eh, Greek opsis and anablepsis)
From Old English gesiht, from the root of see. The Hebrew idiom is the key to the biblical usage: the ordinary phrase for in the sight of is b''ēnē, literally in the eyes of. To do a thing in God's sight is to do it in His eyes, and so the word carries not observation only but judgment — what a thing looks like to the One whose estimate is final.

Biblical Definition

Sight in Scripture means three things which run together: physical seeing, the divine estimate of a matter, and the mode of knowing that faith replaces. The Hebrew idiom governs the middle sense, and the whole history of the kings is written in it — each did that which was right, or evil, in the sight of the LORD. Grace itself is described in the same terms, and the sentence that turns the flood narrative is one of the shortest in Scripture: “But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD” (Gen 6:8). What God's eyes make of a man is the only verdict that will stand, which is why the psalmist submits not only his words but the thoughts behind them to that court: “Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer” (Psa 19:14). Physical sight is one of the great signs of the Messiah's coming, named in the text He read at Nazareth: He was sent “to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised” (Luk 4:18) — and He gave it repeatedly, to men born blind, as a parable of what He does for souls. Yet the Christian's present life is deliberately not conducted by sight, and Paul states the principle in a parenthesis that governs everything around it: “(For we walk by faith, not by sight:)” (2Co 5:7). Sight is promised, not withheld — now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face. It is postponed, and faith is the appointed way of walking until it comes.

Webster 1828 Definition

The act or faculty of seeing; view or notice; the estimate or judgment of one who sees — whence the Hebrew idiom in the sight, that is, in the eyes, of the LORD; and the mode of knowing which faith replaces in this life.

expand to see more

SIGHT, n. 1. The act of seeing; perception of objects by the eye; view.

2. The faculty of vision, or of perceiving objects by the instrumentality of the eyes.

3. Open view; a situation admitting of free view; as, the town lies in sight of the sea.

4. Estimation; judgment; opinion; as, in the sight of God. In Hebrew, in the eyes of.

5. In Scripture, Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD. Gen. 6. We walk by faith, not by sight. 2 Cor. 5.

Key Scripture

Genesis 6:8 — "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD."

Psalm 19:14 — "Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer."

Luke 4:18 — "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted , to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,"

2 Corinthians 5:7 — "(For we walk by faith, not by sight:)"

Modern Corruption

Faith is redefined as a leap taken against evidence, so that walking by faith is made to mean believing without grounds, when Scripture means acting on the testimony of God about things not yet visible.

expand to see more

2Co 5:7 is regularly enlisted to defend a faith held in defiance of evidence — the notion that believing without reasons is the more spiritual act, and that asking for grounds is itself a failure of trust. That is not the contrast Paul draws. His antithesis is not between faith and evidence but between faith and sight: between resting on the testimony of God concerning what is real but not yet visible, and requiring that a thing be present to the eye before it is counted real. Scripture everywhere appeals to grounds. Luke writes so that Theophilus may know the certainty of those things; Peter insists they did not follow cunningly devised fables but were eyewitnesses; Paul lists the resurrection appearances by name and number and stakes the entire faith on whether Christ is risen. Faith in the Bible is a well-founded confidence in a God who has spoken and acted publicly, not a decision to believe without cause.

The mirror-image corruption demands sight now, and it appears wherever a believer's assurance is made to rest on what he can currently see — the visible success of a work, the felt presence of God, health, or prosperity. Scripture warns that this leaves a man at the mercy of his circumstances, and it holds up as its models men who died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off. The principle to recover is that the postponement of sight is temporary and purposeful: God is training a people to trust His word about what is not yet visible, and He will not withhold the sight forever. Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed — a beatitude spoken to men who would themselves see.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'ayin is an eye, and b''ēnē is the idiom in the sight of; mar'eh is an appearance or vision. Greek opsis is appearance or countenance, eidos is that which is seen, and anablepsis is recovery of sight.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'ayin (H5869) — an eye; and by idiom the sight, judgment, or estimate of the one who sees; right in his own eyes (Jdg 21:25).

Hebrew mar'eh (H4758) — sight, appearance, vision; the look of a thing as distinct from what it is.

Greek eidos (G1491) — that which is seen, outward appearance; the word behind sight in 2Co 5:7, so faith is contrasted with mere appearance.

Greek anablepsis (G309) — recovery of sight; used in Luk 4:18 of the Messiah's promised work, from anablepō, to look up or see again.

Greek enōpion (G1799) — before, in the sight of; the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew idiom, as acceptable in thy sight.

Usage

"Of God's estimate as the decisive one: Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD (Gen 6:8)."

"Of submitting heart and speech to that estimate: acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer (Psa 19:14)."

"Of the present mode of the Christian life: we walk by faith, not by sight (2Co 5:7)."
